title: Before Classical Education, There Was New Criticism
author: Annika Hernandez
summary: Annika Hernandez, a former Humane Letters teacher at Chandler Prep, reviews John Guillory's short book On Close Reading and argues that the New Criticism it describes is an intellectual ancestor of much classical literature pedagogy. She notes that classical schools reject content-neutral ELA skills in favor of literary knowledge, yet still depend on close reading for essays and seminars. Drawing on Guillory, she explains that the New Critics of the 1920s sought to make criticism its own discipline, treating works as having 'organic unity' and interpreting them through their form rather than author biography or historical context. Where Guillory calls organic unity an embarrassment, Hernandez argues classical educators would defend formalism pedagogically, illustrating how a biographical lecture on Poe can reduce his stories to symptoms of trauma rather than deliberate artistic choices. Her second point is that the New Critics' definition of close reading as making the reading process visible supplies a rich answer to students who ask why certain books are 'great': great works are dense enough to reward sustained interpretation, as the Iliad does. She closes by noting New Criticism is not the sole influence, since Aristotle's Poetics also shapes the tradition.
points: Hernandez traces classical schools' habit of avoiding historicizing literature to New Criticism's formalist effort to study a work's inner structure rather than external influences.
Front-loading an author's biography, as with Poe's tragic life, can lead students to read works as products of trauma rather than as deliberate artistic choices.
Classical pedagogy borrows the view that great artists transcend their context rather than being reducible to material, psychological, or identity factors.
Guillory's definition of close reading as 'a showing of the work of reading' explains why it pairs naturally with seminar discussion, debate, and analytical writing.
Following I.A. Richards, a book's greatness can be defended by its responsiveness to close reading, which lets teachers justify the canon without appeals to nostalgia or utility.
quotes: Classical schools tend not to subscribe to the skills-based approach to English literature classes, in which students practice content-neutral linguistic tasks like guessing a word’s meaning from context, distinguishing denotation from connotation, or summarizing the main idea of a passage. Classical students are more likely to learn about the symbolism of water in The Miracle Worker, Scrooge’s character development in A Christmas Carol, or the theme of “atavism” in The Call of the Wild—in short, knowledge of literature.

At first glance, the definition of close reading might seem obvious: reading attentively, slowly, and carefully. But, while people have read books attentively for centuries, Guillory is focused on defining a practice belonging to a particular literary movement that emerged in the 1920s: New Criticism. According to Guillory, the New Critics’ novel and controversial approach to literature, eventually named close reading, “permanently transformed literary studies.

One distinctive quality of classical pedagogy is that it avoids historicizing works of literature. While students in a history class may consider how various events and trends shaped a primary source, literature teachers urge their students to remain focused on what’s in the text itself. Classical educators may be interested to learn that this practice has roots in New Criticism.

They believed literary works possess “organic unity,” meaning they’re internally coherent, with all parts contributing harmoniously to an overarching theme. They were formalists, meaning they believed that we can understand a book by studying its content, rather than needing to consult the author’s biography, historical context, or external statements about the work.
Learning about an author’s biography or a book’s historical context can be a distraction; it can burden the reader with assumptions and biases, narrowing the vision.

Borrowing from New Criticism’s formalism, classical schools steer students toward an understanding of authors as careful, deliberate artists who make choices based on what strikes them as good and beautiful rather than being unwittingly shaped by material or psychological forces. They help students to understand that part of what makes an artist great is the ability to transcend his or her context, and they avoid the troubling tendency to reduce authors to their immutable characteristics.
This was the contribution of the New Critics: making reading visible and therefore compatible with writing, discussion, and debate.

In other words, literature is great if it’s dense—if it’s rich and complex enough to invite intense conversation, lively debate, interpretive analysis essays, and other forms of close reading, often across decades or centuries. The Iliad is great, in part, because we’ll never quite settle our questions about the tension between fate and free will in the narrative, the antidote to Achilles’ rage, or what it means for the generations of men to be “as the generation of leaves.
